Thirty-four comments

Triplets

This is tune is triplet-heaven, at least the way I’ve shown it here. You don’t have to play all those triplets - in fact it would be a good idea to vary the ornamentation a lot more - but they can add a nice percussive, rhythmic effect.

↳ Posted by Jeremy on July 30th, 2001.

I’m just watching a webcast of Liz Carroll live, and she adds in a little half-sized (?) part between the A and B parts of “Fermoy Lasses”. It’s really neat, and makes you sit up straight if you’re just expecting the usual lovely Em/G reel. I think her B part’s in A minor or A mixo. Anyone have a clue?

Fermoy Lasses

Does anyone know who wrote this? I saw it attributed to Joe Cooley. Is this correct?

↳ Posted by Sean1798 on July 24th, 2011.

Not possible

Joe Cooley was born in 1924. “Fermoy Lasses” appears in “O’Neill’s 1001 Gems - The Dance Music of Ireland” printed in 1907.

Simpler notation

Micho Russell’s version of The Fermoy Lasses, X:16

Here’s a version I was introduced to by Paul McGrattan during the Ceoltóir course in Ballyfermot. I’ve heard three recordings of Micho Russell playing this tune which I tried to transcribe as well as possible in a simple form. He doesn’t always play it exactly the same way between the recordings. For example I wrote a C at the end of the 6th bar, and I love it because it changes the harmony when you play that C instead of playing the B like at the end of the second bar, which adds a certain dynamique, but Micho Russell doesn’t do it systematically.

Re: The Fermoy Lasses

“…the repeat is written on the score sheet instead of in the player’s memory.”

To repeat or not depends on who you’re playing it with. So in a session, the option very well needs to be in your memory—“Do they play this single or double? Ears open!”

This tune is widely played double (AABB) but also single (ABAB).
